# Results

## Data trimming

The data set for accuracy included 35 participants contained a total of 6720 data points (192 trials x 35 participants) and maintained all correct and incorrect trials. 
Due to an error, three stimulus items were duplicated in the data (two non-cognates and one double cognate) and were subsequently omitted from further analysis, resulting in a total of 6510 data points (186 per participant).
For reaction time the analyzed data frame contained 2180 data points after removing pseudoword trials (n = `r ps_removed`), incorrect trials (n = `r incorrect`), trials that were too fast (n = `r too_fast`) or too slow (n = `r too_slow`). Some trials fit multiple criteria for removal, and a trial was considered too fast or too slow when the reaction time was under 500ms or over 2 seconds.

## Accuracy


```{r accuracy, fig.cap="Percentage of correct responses by word type"}
knitr::include_graphics(here("docs", "plots", "overall_acc.png"))
```

Overall, there was evidence of a cumulative effect of cognate facilitation in accuracy.
Figure \@ref(fig:accuracy) shows the overall accuracy within the entire data set (`r nrow(p_data)` trials) excluding pseudowords (in which `r round2(totals_n$pct_correct[2]*100)`% of trials were correct)
Participants were most accurate for triple cognates (`r round2(totals_n$pct_correct[3]*100)`%), followed by double cognates (`r round2(totals_n$pct_correct[4]*100)`%) and non-cognates were the least accurate (`r round2(totals_n$pct_correct[1]*100)`%).

For most individual participants, cognates were helpful in correctly answered a trial, but there were a few exceptions.
Figure \@ref(fig:accuracyind) shows histograms of individuals' percentage of correct trials in each word-type. 
Individual accuracy in non-cognates ranged from `r round2(range(neat_ind_data$non_cognate)[1])` % of trials correct to `r round2(range(neat_ind_data$non_cognate)[2])`% (median `r round2(median(neat_ind_data$non_cognate))`%).
Like the data set as a whole, the median of individual percentages correct for the triple cognates was the highest: `r round2(median(neat_ind_data$three_way_cognate))`% (range `r round2(range(neat_ind_data$three_way_cognate)[1])`% - `r round2(range(neat_ind_data$three_way_cognate)[2])`%), followed by double cognates (median percentage correct = `r round2(median(neat_ind_data$two_way_cognate))`%; range = `r round2(range(neat_ind_data$two_way_cognate)[1])`% - `r round2(range(neat_ind_data$two_way_cognate)[2])`).
Taken together, these descriptive results suggest that, while most participants benefit from cognates in accuracy, a minority also experience steep drops in accuracy.
Indeed, two participants showed the opposite of expected and were most accurate in non-cognates (60.4% and 68.7%) and much less accurate in two-way (25% and 16.7%) and triple cognates (20.8% and 8.3%).

```{r accuracyind, fig.cap="Histograms of individual percentages corrects by word type"}
knitr::include_graphics(here("docs", "plots", "ind_acc.png"))
```

L3 proficiency, as measured by the adapted LexTALE was more beneficial for accuracy at lower levels of proficiency. 
Figure \@ref(fig:accuracyindpro) shows the change in accuracy for non-cogates relative to both double and triple cognates. 
A positive value on the plot refers to an advantage for that cognate types of the value on the y-axis.
For example, a value of 40 on the y-axis means that a specific participant was 40% more accurate in a cognate condition than non-cognates.
On the other hand, negative values suggest they were less accurate. 
The fitted lines represent the predicted increase in accuracy as proficiency increases. 
The negative slope suggests that as proficiency increases, the relative benefit of cognate status for accuracy diminishes.

```{r accuracyindpro, fig.cap="Increase in accuracy as a function of proficiency and word type"}
knitr::include_graphics(here("docs", "plots", "ind_acc_prof.png"))
```

```{r}
acc_table = describe_posterior(accuracy_mod_b) %>% 
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2))) %>% 
  mutate(CI = paste0("[", CI_low, ", ", CI_high, "]")) %>% 
  mutate(ROPE = paste0("[", ROPE_low, ", ", ROPE_high, "]")) %>% 
  select(Parameter, Median, CI, pd, ROPE, ROPE_Percentage, Rhat, ESS)



acc_t <- flextable(acc_table, use_labels = FALSE) %>% 
  set_caption(caption = "Posterior Distribution of the Accuracy Model") %>% 
  font(fontname = "Times New Roman", part = "all") %>% 
  theme_booktabs() %>% 
  align(align = "center", part = "all") %>% 
  align(j = 1, align = "left", part = "body") %>% 
  set_header_labels(
  CI = "95% CI",
  ROPE_Percentage = "% in ROPE"
) %>% 
  autofit()
  
acc_t
```

The Bayesian Model largely corroborated the descriptive effects.
Overall, there was strong evidence for a general cognate effect in accuracy, and somewhat weaker evidence for a cumulative effect.
Figure \@ref(fig:accmod) visualizes the posterior distribution for the accuracy model and Table 2 includes specific estimates of each model term. 
In this model, the intercept was `r acc_table$Median[1]` and represents the log-odds of an accurate response in the reference condition (double cognates) when the adapted LexTALE scores (proficiency_z) and lexical frequency (frequency_z) are average.
In practice, this corresponds to a participant with average proficiency would be accurate `r round(plogis(acc_table$Median[1]), digits = 3)*100`% of the time for words of average lexical frequency. 
The effect for non-cognates was `r acc_table$Median[2]`, 95% HDI = `r acc_table$CI[2]`, pd = `r acc_table$pd[2]`, which corresponds to a lower predicted probability of a correct response (`r round(plogis(acc_table$Median[1] + acc_table$Median[2]), digits = 3)*100`%).
The probability of direction was 1.00, signaling that virtually the entire posterior distribution is below zero, providing extremely strong evidence for a negative effect.
Additionally, 0% of the posterior distribution fell within the ROPE, suggesting that none of the credible parameter values were practically equivalent to zero.
For triple cognates, the median effect was `r acc_table$Median[3]` 95% HDI = `r acc_table$CI[3]`, indicating that the most credible values of the effect were positive. 
The effect was associated with a pd of `r acc_table$pd[3]`, indicating that approximately 98% of the posterior distribution supported a positive effect. 
Additionally, only `r acc_table$ROPE_Percentage[3]*100`% of the posterior distribution fell within the ROPE, suggesting that most credible parameter values were not practically equivalent to zero. 
Taken together, these results provide evidence that triple cognates were identified more accurately than double cognates, although the evidence was somewhat weaker than that observed for the non-cognate effect.

Higher numbers for both the continuous predictors lexical frequency and proficiency were associated with higher accuracy.
For lexical frequency, the median estimate was `r acc_table$Median[4]`  `r acc_table$CI[4]`, indicating that a one standard deviation increase in lexical frequency was associated with an increase of `r acc_table$Median[4]` in the log-odds of a correct response. 
Holding all other predictors constant, predicted accuracy increases to around `r round(plogis(acc_table$Median[1] + acc_table$Median[4]), digits = 3)*100`% in words that were 1 standard deviation more frequent than average, while it dropped to `r round(plogis(acc_table$Median[1] - acc_table$Median[4]), digits = 3)*100`% for words that were one standard deviation less frequent than average. 
Again, the pd (`r acc_table$pd[4]`) and ROPE percentage (`r acc_table$ROPE_Percentage[4]`%) provide strong evidence for the existence of a positive association between lexical frequency and accuracy. 
Proficiency was also shown the be positively associated with accuracy; the estimate `r acc_table$Median[5]` `r acc_table$CI[5]` suggests that a one standard deviation increase in the adapted LexTALE score was associated with an increase of `r acc_table$Median[5]` increase in the log-odds of a correct response. 
Predicted accuracy increases to around `r round(plogis(acc_table$Median[1] + acc_table$Median[4]), digits = 3)*100`% by participants that were 1 standard deviation more proficient than average, while it dropped to `r round(plogis(acc_table$Median[1] - acc_table$Median[5]), digits = 3)*100`% for participants that were one standard deviation less proficient than average. 
Like frequency, the pd (`r acc_table$pd[5]`) and ROPE percentage (`r acc_table$ROPE_Percentage[5]`) provide compelling evidence of that the effect is positive and not negligible. 

## Reaction time

Like accuracy, the analysis of the reaction time data showed evidence of a general cognate facilitation effect. 
Figure \@ref(fig:overt) shows the overall mean reaction times in milliseconds in for each word type. 
Non-cognate words were recognized as real words slowest (mean reaction time `r round2(report_rt$mean_rt[2]*1000)`ms, sd = `r round2(report_rt$sd_log_rt[2]*1000)`), while both two-way (`r round2(report_rt$mean_rt[1]*1000)`ms, sd = `r round2(report_rt$sd_log_rt[1]*1000)`) and triple cognates were recognized faster `r round2(report_rt$mean_rt[3]*1000)`ms, sd = `r round2(report_rt$sd_log_rt[3]*1000)`.
The difference in reaction time between two-way and triple cognates was quite small (d = .03).

In the case of reaction time, there were even more pronounced differences regarding individual differences. 
Figure \@ref(fig:indrt) shows individual effect sizes in three situations: going from double to triple cognates, non-cognates to double cognates, and non-cognates to triple cognates. 
It was predicted that if there was a cumulative effect of cognate facilitation, that double to triple cognates would yield negative effects. 
However, many participants were faster (`r pos_neg_cumu$n[2]` of 35) in double cognates than triple cognates, while the remaining `r pos_neg_cumu$n[1]` participants showed the opposite pattern and processed triple cognates fastest.  
The second facet shows the individual effects for non-cognates relative to double cognates.  
In this instance, as expected, most participants (`r pos_neg_dub$n[1]`) were faster for double cognates than non-cognates, although `r pos_neg_dub$n[1]` individuals were not. 
Similar proportions of participants were also faster at deciding that triple cognates were real words (`r pos_neg_trip$n[1]`).
Taken together, these results suggest that while most individuals showed descriptive evidence general cognate effects in reaction time, there was not strong evidence for a cumulative effect in which triple cognates were processed faster than double cognates. 

Unlike accuracy, there was no descriptive evidence regarding a relationship between differences in reaction time and L3 proficiency. 
Figure \@ref(fig:indrtprof) shows the individual effect sizes for non-cognates to double cognates, non-cognates to triple cognates, and cumulative (double cognate to triple cognates).
A negative value in this case indicates that a specific participant was faster in the latter conditon (e.g. a negative value for non-cognates to double cognates would show that the participant reacted faster on average to double cognates).
The relatively flat slopes on the fitted lines in each case suggests that the mangnitude of effects does not vary by proficiency level. 

```{r overt, fig.cap="Mean reaction time of each word type"}
knitr::include_graphics(here("docs", "plots", "over_rt.png"))

```


```{r indrt, fig.cap="Individual effects in reaction times"}
knitr::include_graphics(here("docs", "plots", "ind_rt.png"))

```



```{r}
rt_table = describe_posterior(l3_model_rt, rope_range = c(-0.0065, 0.0065)) %>% 
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2))) %>% 
  mutate(CI = paste0("[", CI_low, ", ", CI_high, "]")) %>% 
  mutate(ROPE = paste0("[", ROPE_low, ", ", ROPE_high, "]")) %>% 
  select(Parameter, Median, CI, pd, ROPE, ROPE_Percentage, Rhat, ESS)



rt_t <- flextable(rt_table, use_labels = FALSE) %>% 
  set_caption(caption = "Posterior Distribution of the Reaction Time Model") %>% 
  font(fontname = "Times New Roman", part = "all") %>% 
  theme_booktabs() %>% 
  align(align = "center", part = "all") %>% 
  align(j = 1, align = "left", part = "body") %>% 
  set_header_labels(
  CI = "95% CI",
  ROPE_Percentage = "% in ROPE"
) %>% 
  autofit()
  
rt_t
```

The Bayesian model largely corroborated the descriptive results for reaction time.
Figure \@ref(fig:retmod) visualized the posterior distribution of the Bayesian model while Table 3 provides additional details regarding the posterior shape and fit.
The intercept term of this model (`r rt_table$Median[1]`) corresponds to the log reaction time of a double cognate of average frequency by a participant with average proficiency. 
This value corresponds to `r round2(exp(rt_table$Median[1])*1000)` milliseconds. 
The non-cognate model term is `r rt_table$Median[2]` `r rt_table$CI[2]` and indicates a slow down relative to double cognates of about `r round2(abs(exp(rt_table$Median[1])*1000 - exp(rt_table$Median[2])*1000))` milliseconds. 
triple cognates were predicted to be processed slightly faster that double cognates (`r rt_table$Median[3]` `r rt_table$CI[3]`), but had both positive and negative plausible estimates in the posterior distribution, as well as a relatively low pd (`r rt_table$pd[3]`) and `r rt_table$ROPE_percentage[3]*100`% in the ROPE. 
Lexical frequency was a strong predictor of reaction time.
Like with accuracy, the model term represents the change in reaction time for a one standard deviation increase in frequency and in this case predicts faster reactions (`r rt_table$Median[4]` `r rt_table$CI[4]`) in more frequent words corresponding to `round2(abs(exp(rt_table$Median[1])*1000 - exp(rt_table$Median[4])*1000))` milliseconds.
Finally, the adapted LexTALE score (proficiency) was associated with a slight speedup in processing, but this difference did not fall completely outside the ROPE (`r rt_table$Median[5]` `r rt_table$CI[5]`), rendering the effect inconclusive. 
Taken together, the results of the model point to a general cognate effect that is not explained by proficiency and with lexical frequency held constant. 
Importantly, the model does not support a cumulative effect in lexical decisions.
